title: Sirolimus plus roxadustat synergistically enhances immunosuppression and erythropoiesis in pure red cell aplasia: a multicenter trial

sections.abstract:
Acquired pure red cell aplasia (aPRCA) is rare and challenging to treat. We investigated the efficacy and safety of sirolimus plus roxadustat in patients with aPRCA (Chinese Clinical Trial Register number, ChiCTR2200065107). We enrolled 82 patients with aPRCA in this prospective single-arm, open-label, multicenter trial between October 2022 and January 2024. Treatment response and safety files were evaluated. The median age was 63 years. Seven patients withdrew during the trial period. Sirolimus plus roxadustat produced an overall response (OR) in 65 patients (90.3%) 3 months after initiation, which included a complete response (CR) in 39 (54.2%) and a partial response in 26 (36.1%). The 3-month CR rate was significantly higher in the newly diagnosed group (65.9% vs. 38.7%; P = 0.022). The 6-month OR rate in the entire cohort was 93.0% (CR, 77.5%; PR, 15.5%). The mean hemoglobin concentration increased from 5.5 ± 1.6 g/dL at baseline to 11.6 ± 2.5 g/dL after 6 months of treatment. The proportions of patients who achieved transfusion independence within 1, 2, and 3 months of treatment were 57.4%, 76.6%, and 89.5%, respectively. The Functional Assessment of Chronic Illness Therapy-Fatigue Scale score and SF-36 survey score significantly improved after treatment. Treatment-related adverse events occurred in 24 patients (29.2%), and four events (4.9%) were grade ≥3. Sirolimus plus roxadustat is a promising treatment for aPRCA and has an acceptable safety profile, which warrants further investigation in a randomized setting.

Subject terms: Clinical trial design, Haematological diseases
sections.introduction:
Pure red cell aplasia (PRCA) is a rare syndrome characterized by normocytic normochromic anemia, reticulocytopenia, and paucity or absence of erythroid progenitors in the bone marrow. 1 Acquired PRCA (aPRCA) may be primary or secondary to various drugs and chemicals, ABO-mismatched allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation, or conditions such as malignancy, autoimmune disease, viral infection, and pregnancy. Most cases of aPRCA are idiopathic and likely caused by the destruction of erythroid precursors by cytotoxic T cells. 1 , 2

Immunosuppressive therapy is the cornerstone of treatment and can achieve remission in most patients. 1 , 2 In a 2023 meta-analysis of aPRCA treatment, 3 cyclosporine A (CsA) was the most frequently used immunosuppressant. When used as a first-line treatment, it provided an overall response (OR) rate of 73%. First-line treatment using corticosteroid (Cs) monotherapy provided an OR rate of 47%. 3 Patients who fail to respond to CsA, Cs, CsA + Cs, or other treatments, such as cyclophosphamide (CTX), methotrexate (MTX), antithymocyte globulin (ATG) or bone marrow transplantation, can be considered. 1 , 4 – 7 Anti-CD20 and anti-CD52 monoclonal antibodies have also been reported to induce remission of therapy-resistant PRCA. 1 , 4 , 8 – 12

Sirolimus is a lipophilic macrolide antibiotic derived from Streptomyces hygroscopicus that inhibits mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR). It has been used to prevent posttransplant organ rejection and treat autoimmune diseases. 13 – 16 Sirolimus is efficacious in aPRCA and appears to be promising in relapsed/refractory (R/R) aPRCA. 17 – 19 Roxadustat is a hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) prolyl hydroxylase inhibitor that mimics the natural response to hypoxia. It was initially approved for the treatment of anemia in chronic kidney disease. 20 , 21 In lower-risk myelodysplastic syndrome, roxadustat is effective for treating anemia and has an acceptable safety profile. 22 Recent studies have suggested that crosstalk occurs between the HIF and mTOR signaling pathways. Under hypoxic conditions, activation of Hif-1α requires mTOR activity. 23 , 24 That is, mTOR is an upstream activator of HIF-1α function. 25 Sirolimus, an mTOR inhibitor, has been suggested to suppress the expression and function of HIF-1 in cancer cells. 26 aPRCA is characterized by two core pathologies: immune-mediated destruction of erythroid progenitors and inadequate erythropoiesis. When the mTOR pathway inhibitor sirolimus is used as monotherapy to suppress T-cell immune function for PRCA treatment, it might simultaneously inhibit downstream HIF function, thereby affecting red blood cell production. Adding roxadustat to sirolimus monotherapy might overcome the impact of sirolimus on HIF that leads to insufficient erythropoiesis, thereby creating a synergistic effect to promote red blood cell production.

We hypothesized that the addition of roxadustat to sirolimus might provide clinical benefit in aPRCA and performed a prospective single-arm multicenter clinical trial (ChiCTR2200065107) for evaluation.
sections.methods:
Patients diagnosed with aPRCA between October 2022 and January 2024 at ten hospitals in China were eligible for study inclusion. The diagnostic workup was based on an approach described by Gurnari and Maciejewki. 31 A detailed history of drug use and exposure to toxins and infections was obtained, and patients underwent evaluations of heart, liver, and kidney function; virological examination (cytomegalovirus, Epstein–Barr virus, parvovirus B19 DNA); and bone marrow examination (morphology; analyses of chromosomes, immunotype, and T-cell receptor gene rearrangement; and marrow biopsy). Computed tomography and/or magnetic resonance imaging was performed to evaluate thymoma and other neoplasms.

The trial inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) age ≥ 18 and ≤80 years; (2) diagnosis of aPRCA (both newly diagnosed and R/R types); (3) cardiac ejection fraction ≥45%; and (4) total bilirubin, alanine aminotransferase, and aspartate aminotransferase concentrations ≤3 times the upper limit of their respective reference ranges. We excluded patients with uncontrolled underlying disease, active infection, severe disease-related complications, active malignancy, or mental illness. Pregnant or nursing women were also excluded.

The study was approved by the institutional ethics committee of Soochow Hopes Hematonosis Hospital, the First Affiliated Hospital of Soochow University (No. 2022011) and was performed in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. All patients provided written informed consent.

Sirolimus was initiated at a dosage of 0.03 mg/kg/day and then adjusted according to regular concentration monitoring. The target concentration was 4 to 12 ng/mL. Sirolimus was tapered and discontinued in patients who responded after 24 months of maintenance therapy. Roxadustat was initiated at a dose of 70 mg three times a week. The use of immunosuppressive agents such as CsA, CTX, MTX, tacrolimus, ATG and other immunosuppressive treatments was prohibited throughout the trial. Cs were only permitted when indicated to treat symptoms of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, asthma, or severe allergic reactions. Use of recombinant human erythropoietin or luspatercept was not permitted. In patients who maintained a hemoglobin concentration ≥12 g/dL for 4 weeks, the dose of roxadustat was tapered gradually and stopped; those with a hemoglobin concentration <11 g/dL continued treatment for at least 52 weeks. Patient follow-up was conducted every week for the first 3 months and then every 2 weeks until the end of the study. The follow-up visits comprised a patient interview, physical examination, organ function assessment, and laboratory testing, including blood cell and reticulocyte counts. Serum ferritin and erythropoietin were evaluated every 3 months. All patients completed at least 6 months of treatment.

Blood transfusions were performed in patients with symptomatic anemia or hemoglobin concentrations <6 g/dL. Supportive care and treatment of infection were provided as necessary. Patients were able to discontinue treatment or withdraw from the study at any time for any reason.

The Functional Assessment of Chronic Illness Therapy-Fatigue Scale 33 was used to evaluate fatigue at baseline and then monthly for 6 months after treatment (score range, 0–52; higher scores indicate less fatigue). Quality of life was assessed using the SF-36 survey at baseline and 6 months after treatment (eight subscales with scores ranging from 0–100; higher scores represent better health and functioning).

Efficacy was assessed 3 and 6 months after treatment. CR was defined as a hemoglobin concentration >12 g/dL in men and >11 g/dL in women that lasted for at least 2 months. PR was defined as a > 3 g/dL increase in hemoglobin concentration compared with baseline and transfusion independence in a patient who did not meet the criteria for CR. 19 OR was defined as either CR or PR. No response (NR) was defined as neither CR nor PR. Changes in hemoglobin concentration and quality of life and achievement of transfusion independence after treatment were also evaluated. Safety was assessed by monitoring the incidence and severity of adverse events throughout the trial. Treatment-related adverse events were graded using the National Cancer Institute common terminology criteria. The relationship of events to the study drug was judged by the investigator.

Continuous variables are expressed as the means with standard deviation or medians with range and were compared using the t test or Mann–Whitney U test as appropriate. Categorical variables are expressed as frequencies with percentages and were compared using the χ 2 or Fisher exact test as appropriate. P < 0.05 was considered significant. Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS software (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA) and Prism software (GraphPad, Boston, MA, USA).
sections.results:
Eighty-two aPRCA patients who met the criteria were enrolled. Patient characteristics are shown in Table 1 . The median age was 63 years, and 45 patients were men (54.9%). aPRCA was classified as primary in 65 patients (79.3%) and secondary in 17 (20.7%). It was also classified as newly diagnosed in 44 patients (53.7%) and R/R in 38 patients (46.3%). Previous treatment approaches were unsuccessful for 11 patients: four who were treated with CsA alone, two with CsA + Cs, two with tacrolimus alone, one with tacrolimus + Cs, and two with CTX + Cs. Twenty-seven patients initially responded to immunosuppressive therapy but subsequently relapsed.

Baseline characteristics of the enrolled patients

Hb hemoglobin

Three patients discontinued treatment because of adverse reactions, including one with elevated liver transaminases (mainly alanine aminotransferase, grade 2) after 21 days of treatment and two with elevated liver transaminases (grade 1) after 14 days. These three patients did not reach the protocol-specified timepoint for efficacy assessment (3 months of treatment) and were therefore excluded from the efficacy analysis. However, all three were included in the safety analysis, and their adverse events have been comprehensively reported in our safety data. Seven patients (8.5%) withdrew from the trial. The cause of withdrawal was personal reasons in two patients and the high cost of treatment in three patients; the other two patients did not cooperate with sirolimus concentration monitoring and were lost to follow-up. Therefore, 72 patients were included in the final efficacy analysis. Until the last follow-up, death occurred in four patients, and two patients experienced relapse and were switched to other therapies.

The median duration of sirolimus plus roxadustat treatment was 557 days (range, 123–717). The response of the entire cohort at 3 and 6 months is shown in Table 2 . Sirolimus plus roxadustat produced an OR in 65 patients (90.3%) 3 months after initiation: complete response (CR) in 39 (54.2%) and partial response (PR) in 26 (36.1%). The 3-month OR rate was comparable between the newly diagnosed and R/R groups (92.7% and 87.1%, respectively; P = 0.428). However, the 3-month CR rate was significantly higher in the newly diagnosed group (65.9% vs. 38.7%; P = 0.022).

The 6-month OR rate was 93.0% (CR, 77.5%; PR, 15.5%) in the entire cohort and did not significantly differ between the newly diagnosed and R/R groups (95.1% and 90.0%, respectively; P = 0.405). The 6-month CR rate was slightly higher in the newly diagnosed group (85.4% vs. 66.7%); however, the difference was not significant ( P = 0.062). The time to response and efficacy are shown in Fig. 1a, b . The median time to response in the entire cohort was 35.5 days (range, 10–180). The median time to CR was 76 days (range, 30–390).

The mean hemoglobin concentration increased from 5.5 ± 1.6 g/dL at baseline to 11.6 ± 2.5 g/dL after 6 months of treatment (Fig. 1c ; P < 0.001). Among the 47 patients who required a red blood cell transfusion before treatment initiation, the proportions of patients who achieved transfusion independence within 1, 2, and 3 months of treatment were 57.4%, 76.6%, and 89.5%, respectively. The reticulocyte count increased temporarily in the first month after treatment and then gradually decreased to normal fluctuating levels (Fig. 1d ). Compared with baseline, erythropoietin concentration decreased from 1040 ± 712 ng/mL to 161 ± 188 ng/mL (Fig. 1e ; P < 0.0001), and serum ferritin decreased from 1645 ± 2360 ng/mL to 582 ± 449 ng/mL (Fig. 1f ; P < 0.0001) after 6 months of treatment.

The response to sirolimus plus roxadustat in primary PRCA is shown in Table 3 . The OR rates at 3 and 6 months were 87.5% and 90.9%, respectively. The 6-month OR rate did not significantly differ between primary aPRCA patients who received the regimen as first-line treatment and those who received it as second-line treatment (94.3% and 85.0%, respectively; P = 0.342).

Treatment-related adverse events occurred in 24 patients (29.2%) and are shown in Table 4 . Fifteen cases of oral mucositis resolved with oral antibiotics and supportive care. Three patients developed elevated creatinine concentrations, but treatment was not discontinued; after supportive treatment, the concentration was maintained within the upper limit of the reference range. Patients with grade 1–2 adverse events underwent a decrease in the sirolimus dose or discontinuation until the reaction resolved. Four cases (4.9%) of pneumonia were classified as grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events; these occurred 3.6, 6.9, 13.2, and 13.8 months after exposure to the combination regimen, respectively. The four patients who contracted pneumonia were relatively older (median age, 69.5 years; maximum age, 75 years) and had prolonged prior exposure to other immunosuppressants before initiating the combination regimen. All events were managed with broad-spectrum antibiotics and temporary discontinuation of sirolimus. Two patients were hospitalized owing to pneumonia and recovered; the other two died from mixed bacterial and fungal pneumonia.

sections.discussion:
The mTOR pathway is a critical regulator of cell growth, proliferation, and, importantly, T-cell activation. Sirolimus, an inhibitor of mTOR, is used to prevent rejection after solid organ transplantation and has been shown to be beneficial in treating chronic immune thrombocytopenia and cytopenias. 16 , 27 , 28 The evidence regarding the use of sirolimus to treat aPRCA is limited to two small case series 17 , 18 and a prospective study of 64 patients with R/R aPRCA. 19 Roxadustat is effective for treating anemia of chronic kidney disease 21 and reduces the incidence of transfusion in patients with lower-risk myelodysplastic syndrome. 22 It has not been formally evaluated in aPRCA patients. Cumulative evidence has suggested that sirolimus inhibits mTORC1, reducing HIF-1α translation and expression, which results in impaired red cell production. 23 , 24 We hypothesized that roxadustat would exert a synergistic effect when combined with sirolimus in patients with aPRCA. In our prospective study, sirolimus plus roxadustat as first-line treatment in newly diagnosed aPRCA provided an OR rate of 95.1% after 6 months of treatment. For R/R aPRCA, the corresponding rate was 90.0%, which is similar to the 84.7% 6-month OR rate reported in a previous prospective study of sirolimus monotherapy as second-line treatment in patients with R/R aPRCA. 19 The median time to response in R/R aPRCA in our study was 41 days, and the 3-month OR rate was 87.1%, which suggests a potential clinical benefit of combined treatment.

CsA, Cs, and CsA + Cs are all effective as first-line treatments for primary aPRCA, yielding response rates ranging from 43% to 86%. 3 , 5 , 29 , 30 Although highly effective, Cs do not produce a durable response and are associated with long-term side effects. 1 , 5 , 31 CsA-containing regimens are associated with significantly longer relapse-free survival than Cs. 5 Previous studies have found that in patients with newly diagnosed aPRCA, the time to response for CsA monotherapy and corticosteroid monotherapy was 82 days 65 and days, respectively. 5 Our combined regimen demonstrated a response time of 33.5 days, suggesting that it is a promising approach and merits evaluation in a randomized controlled trial. Transfusion dependence is common in aPRCA. Immunosuppressive therapy usually requires several months to take effect. Until then, red blood cell transfusion has been the only option for treating anemia, which is associated with potential adverse clinical consequences. Transfusion independence was achieved in 57.4% of our patients within 1 month and in 89.5% within 3 months. In a national study of primary aPRCA patients from Japan, the 3- and 6-month rates of transfusion independence after CsA monotherapy were 78% and 89%, respectively. 5 These findings suggest that combined treatment with roxadustat + sirolimus is associated with a higher rate of transfusion independence than CsAs. In addition, patient-reported scores of fatigue and quality of life improved after combined treatment. However, because of our study’s single-arm, open-label design, these improvements should be interpreted with caution. They require rigorous validation in randomized controlled trials.

Sirolimus plus roxadustat was safe and well tolerated in aPRCA. The most common treatment-related adverse event was infection (oral mucositis and pneumonia), as has been previously reported with sirolimus monotherapy. 19 The occurrence of mucositis was considered related to the sirolimus concentration, and symptoms improved after dose reduction, analgesic symptomatic treatment, and immunomodulatory therapy. Four cases of pneumonia, all considered to be treatment-related grade ≥3 adverse events, warrant attention. It is noteworthy that among these four patients, three had relapsed with PRCA after cyclosporine-based therapy, and one had refractory disease. They were relatively older and had received prolonged immunosuppressant treatment before initiating the combination regimen—the shortest immunosuppressant treatment duration was 30 months. Additionally, one patient had comorbid diabetes, another had chronic kidney disease, and yet another had concurrent chronic cardiac insufficiency. Following pneumonia onset, all four were managed with a dose decrease and then discontinuation of sirolimus. Although broad-spectrum antibiotics were administered, the outcome in two patients was unsatisfactory. Sirolimus was not the direct cause of pneumonia, but considering that sirolimus-induced immunosuppression may be a synergistic predisposing factor for pulmonary infection, the impact of sirolimus cannot be completely ruled out. Therefore, we still consider pneumonia to be possibly associated with the administration of sirolimus. Three patients experienced mildly or moderately elevated creatinine concentrations. After dose adjustment or supportive treatment, the concentration decreased to approximately the upper limit of the reference range. Elevated creatinine concentration was not an exclusion criterion for study enrollment, and as previously reported, 18 , 19 no cases of acute kidney injury occurred. As expected with mTOR inhibition, the increases in blood glucose and lipid concentrations were considered drug-related effects of sirolimus itself. Hyperlipidemia was a frequent adverse event (13 patients, 15.9%) and was considered grade 2 in seven patients; management with atorvastatin was effective. For patients with metabolic abnormalities, we increased the monitoring frequency and provided symptomatic treatment. No patients required treatment discontinuation because of adverse events. The median duration of sirolimus plus roxadustat treatment was 557 days, and two patients experienced aPRCA relapse. Studies with longer follow-up are warranted to better assess the risk of relapse.

The mechanism by which sirolimus plus roxadustat affects the immune system remains unclear. Sirolimus promotes immune tolerance by upregulating FOXP3 expression in regulatory T cells, 32 which has a suppressive effect on T-cell activation. Sirolimus causes an increase in regulatory T cells in aPRCA; the number of total T cells, total B cells, and NK cells does not change significantly. 17 We observed a significant decrease in the number of activated T cells (CD3 + CD69 + ) after treatment (Supplementary Fig. 1a–h ). The function of B cells, as assessed by quantitative IgG, IgA, or IgM, did not significantly decrease. However, the concentrations of serum complement C3 and C4 were significantly elevated after treatment (Supplementary Fig. 2a–e ). The combination of sirolimus (mTOR inhibitor) and roxadustat (HIF stabilizer) represents an innovative approach based on the intricate relationship between mTOR signaling and HIF stability. 23 – 26 Of course, this is a mechanistically hypothesis-driven exploratory study, and future in-depth research will be needed in the future for confirmation.

This pilot study is limited by its single-arm, open-label design and lack of a control group. Future studies with uniform patient selection, control groups, and longer follow-up are warranted.
